lesson.title: Sockets That Remember: Building a TCP Connection
lesson.summary: A TCP socket is a Berkeley sockets API socket created for reliable, connection-oriented communication, and its server and client sides follow two different, complementary call sequences.
lesson.body:
A TCP socket is what you get when a program creates a socket of type SOCK_STREAM in the Berkeley sockets API. Underneath, it is backed by everything TCP provides: a reliable, ordered byte stream, built on the handshaking, acknowledgment, and retransmission mechanisms that make that reliability possible.

Because TCP is connection-oriented, using a TCP socket involves a lifecycle, and that lifecycle looks different depending on whether the program is playing the role of server or client. On the server side, the sequence is socket() to create the socket, bind() to attach it to a known local address, listen() to mark it as ready to receive incoming connection attempts, and then accept(), called repeatedly, to pull individual client connections off one at a time, each call producing a brand new socket dedicated to that one client. On the client side, the sequence is much shorter: socket() followed by connect(), reaching out to the server's address, after which that same socket can immediately be used to send and receive data, since connect() is what carries out the handshake.

A simple echo server makes this concrete. The server creates a TCP socket, binds it to port 9000 on its machine, calls listen() to open up a backlog queue for incoming attempts, and then calls accept(), which blocks until a client shows up. Meanwhile, a client program creates its own TCP socket and calls connect() to the server's address at port 9000. That call triggers the three-way handshake, and once it completes, the server's blocked accept() call returns, handing back a brand new socket dedicated entirely to this one client. From there both sides call send() and recv() to exchange bytes, with the server echoing back whatever it receives, until either side closes the connection.

It is worth flagging that listen() and accept() only apply to the server side, and only make sense at all because of TCP's connection oriented model, which is exactly why they get their own dedicated chapters just ahead. It is also worth noting that the same listening socket can be used to accept many different clients over time, one after another, and each of those clients gets its own separate connected socket, so the server can serve many clients at once without their data streams ever getting mixed up with each other.
